chapter: Influences, Los Angeles scene and technique
title: Separate scenes and segregated musicians' unions in Los Angeles
summary: Hollywood West Coast jazz was separate from the black scene on Central Avenue, partly because of separate white and black unions before they merged as Local 47.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Yeah, Shorty Rogers and the Bud Shank and everything, that was up in Hollywood, way up, but the stuff that was happening down in L.A., that was the Minguses and Dexter Gordons and the Sonny Clarks. That was a whole different scene.

Oh, very separate, very separate, because even at that time there was separate unions. Everybody – there was the white union and there was the black union. You couldn’t play at this area if you didn’t belong to that union. You had to be white to play there, or blah blah blah.
I understand Buddy had a big impact on the – combining those.

Yeah. It took a while before they combined and made Local 47. It was different. It was the same thing with Rosemary’s Uncle Ernie. Uncle Ernie was playing with Benny Goodman. They wanted him to go – come and play with Duke [Ellington], but in order for him to play with Duke, he had to leave the white union and join the black union. He felt he was going to lose all his gigs, and so he couldn’t do it, because it was – in those days, it was always a black union and a white union.
